I got the call at half past twelve. Forty-one boxes under seal, discharge stopped, and a master who wanted to know whether he was going to be arrested. He was not. Nothing on board was wrong. What was wrong was on paper. I had the containers surveyed that same afternoon, because until somebody physically opens one, everything you say to the authority is an opinion. Then I had the discrepancy traced back to the loading port, and it took about two hours to find it: a clerk had amended the stowage plan by hand after the bill of lading was already issued. Nobody was hiding anything. Somebody was tidying up. I got the whole set reissued overnight and had it lodged first thing on the Monday. Clearance came back on the Tuesday. Seventy-one hours, and not one of them was about the cargo.

People imagine that we spend the day opening boxes. We do not. Most of what we do is comparison. We take the bill of lading, the manifest and the stowage plan, and we read them against each other, and if the three of them tell the same story the ship goes on working. When they do not, the operation stops until somebody explains why. In this case the bill said machinery parts in transit and the stowage plan put those same containers in a hold that had been declared empty on arrival. That is not a small clerical difference. On paper the cargo had two destinations and one of them was ours. We sealed the boxes rather than opening them, precisely because the problem was documentary. And I will say the thing every inspector says: have your papers reconciled before you arrive. Nobody has ever been detained for a document that agreed with itself.
